Chapter 1: Rethinking Leadership—Why Coaching Matters in Everyday Work
You know, in so many organizations, leadership is often seen as having all the answers. Managers and team leads are expected to swoop in, solve problems, and just keep things moving along. Sound familiar?
But here’s the thing—when leaders always take charge and fix things, it can actually hold everyone back. People start relying on the boss to figure it all out, growth slows down, and let’s be honest, everyone—leaders included—ends up feeling pretty overwhelmed.
The real heart of great leadership isn’t about quick fixes or being the hero. It’s about making a shift—from always directing, to coaching with curiosity. That means helping your team find their own answers rather than handing them solutions.
Now, when I say “coaching,” I’m not talking about some big, formal process that eats up your calendar. Coaching can happen in the hallway, over a quick call, or in those spontaneous, everyday moments. It’s about weaving coaching into your regular conversations, asking a great question here or there, and giving people space to think for themselves.
There are a few core beliefs that really shape this approach:
First, coaching is for everyone—not just for those official sessions behind closed doors. It can happen anywhere, any time.
Second, asking questions is almost always more powerful than giving advice. Sure, jumping in with an answer might solve the issue for now, but you miss out on helping someone learn and grow for next time.
And third, when you empower others to find their own solutions, you’ll see people become more engaged, more invested, and honestly, more capable.
Picture this: a team member comes to you with a problem. Instead of offering a fix right away, you pause, and ask a thoughtful question. Just like that, a typical conversation turns into a real moment of learning. Over time, these small moments add up and start to shape a culture where people feel heard, challenged, and genuinely supported.
Of course, shifting away from being the “fixer” isn’t always easy. It’s a habit built up over years—maybe even decades—of wanting to be helpful. But constantly providing answers? That only creates bottlenecks, limits creativity, and runs leaders ragged.
Building a coaching habit is about stepping back, listening more, and trusting your team to step up. It’s not about doing less—it’s about leading smarter.
To make this shift work, leaders need some practical tools and a clear framework. And that’s exactly what’s coming up. In the next chapters, you’ll get a set of simple yet powerful questions and practical habits to make coaching part of your day—even when things get busy.
So, why does coaching matter? Because it can transform not just individuals, but whole teams and organizations. And it all starts with that first, curious question.
